newsitem.title: UK: Bosnian Serb leader says he's ready to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leader says he's ready to cooperate.

text.p: The Serb member of Bosnia's new three-man presidency, who sparked an angry reaction by boycotting its ceremonial first meeting, now says he is prepared to cooperate, BBC World Service radio reported on Tuesday.

Momcilo Krajisnik stayed away from last Saturday's first meeting in Sarajevo of the collective presidency and the United States threatened new sanctions unless the Bosnian Serbs agreed to comply with the Dayton peace accords.

But in a British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) interview, Krajisnik said he was ready to sign a declaration pledging to defend the constitution of post-war Bosnia and would recommend Serb members of Bosnia's newly-elected assembly to do the same.
"I have the intention that I should send this to the other representatives of the assembly and, if they agree, that we should sign it at a ceremony," he told the BBC.
The declaration was signed on Saturday by the Moslem and Croat members of the three-person presidency.
Foreign dignitaries waited more than three hours on Saturday for Serb representatives to appear at the ceremony in Sarajevo, but they failed to show up.
The Serb boycott of the presidency meeting and inaugural session of the new parliament cast a shadow over prospects for a post-war government.

Krajisnik, who had voiced worries about the safety of Serbs going to Sarajevo, said he wanted any new ceremony to be held on Bosnian Serb territory but the next move was up to international mediator Carl Bildt.

"We're waiting for an initiative from Mr Bildt," he told the BBC. "If he proposes that there should be a meeting of the joint presidency or the constitution of the joint organs, then we accept that, we want that to happen as soon as possible.
"The reasons for us not coming (to Sarajevo) should be respected," he said, referring to Serb concerns about their safety in Sarajevo, which was besieged by Bosnian Serb guns during the 43-month war.
The Dayton pact created a single Bosnian state divided into a Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb republic, but Serbs have continued to proclaim their goal of creating their own state.
The international community wants Bosnia to set up joint institutions including a presidency, parliament, central bank and supreme court, following elections on September 14.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said earlier that the United States was "furious" with the boycott of "an important, symbolic event which was meant to kick off a new era in Bosnia" and Krajisnik had been handed a "very stiff" U.S. letter.

"This letter put Krajisnik and his colleagues on notice that we expect them to take steps rapidly -- in the next couple of days -- to demonstrate their commitment ... to the peace process, to the Dayton accords," Burns said in Washington.
